The report, titled "Insights on Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification in Carbon Pricing: Developing Effective and Inclusive MRV Systems," examines how justice and inclusion can be fostered in the design and implementation of MRV systems. MRV may sound like a highly technical part of carbon pricing, and it is, but technical systems are often not socially neutral. Who informs their design, who can comply and benefit from them, all matter for equity and inclusion. Gender equity, social inclusion, and just transition, therefore, need to reach within the technical architecture of climate policy, not sit alongside of it. This is one practical example of what it means to mainstream inclusion and just transition into our work. We found that MRV systems largely have not yet put gender equality, social inclusion, and just transition principles into practice in their governance arrangements. As a result, there's little documented evidence that MRV design has included inclusive governance mechanisms, such as meaningful stakeholder engagement or tripartite social dialogue. The benefits of MRV are also unevenly accessible, with smaller, less resourced entities and workers facing more difficulty to convert compliance into competitive advantage. Our study found that participatory approaches to MRV can strengthen community ownership, improve data quality, and build technical capacity, extending equity and inclusion to the growing MRV workforce and helping to ensure a more diverse range of workers acquire these increasingly valuable skills. More broadly, a just transition lens can operate not only at the level of workers and communities, but also among states, helping to ensure that all countries have a voice in shaping international standards. We'd be happy to share more about this work, and I encourage people to reach out to IISD if they're interested in the topic. To my original point, this is only one very small area of a very big issue. However, even if we have a 10-course meal in front of us, we can only eat it one bite at a time. We need practical ways to address macro issues at the micro level. In this way, we can plant seeds of progress that give us motivation to work harder and continue. So this is a simple example of how we are doing this and how others can do this. I encourage my colleagues and stakeholders and governments in the room to continue to embed just transition and inclusion in all your areas of work.
